entry.title: Local transversals to a regular foliation
entry.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation of codimension $q$ on a smooth $n$-manifold $M$, with tangent distribution $D=TF$. A subset $T\subseteq M$ is a **local transversal to $F$ at $x\in T$** when $T$ is an embedded submanifold of $M$ of dimension $q$ containing $x$ with $T_xM=D_x\oplus T_xT$. Equivalently $T_xT$ is a linear complement of $D_x$ in $T_xM$; because $\dim T=q=\operatorname{codim}F$, the sum condition is automatically direct. The definition is local: it is a condition at the single point $x$.
entry.strategy: Specialise the published vocabulary: $F$ is a regular foliation atlas, and its tangent distribution $D$ is the smooth rank-$(n-q)$ subbundle supplied by the correspondence theorem. The tangent space $T_xT$ is that of an embedded submanifold, and $\operatorname{codim}F=q$. The dimension hypothesis $q$ is stated explicitly so that transversality is exactly the direct-sum condition and a codimension-one submanifold meeting a leaf tangentially is excluded. No choice principle is used beyond the standing $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the smooth-distribution setting.

entry.title: Leafwise paths and leafwise homotopy relative to endpoints
entry.statement: Let $F$ be a regular foliation of $M$. A **leafwise path** for $F$ is a continuous map $a:[0,1]\to M$ whose image is contained in a single leaf of $F$. A **leafwise homotopy relative to endpoints** between leafwise paths $a,b$ with the same endpoints $x,y$ is a continuous map $H:[0,1]^2\to M$ with $H(0,t)=a(t)$, $H(1,t)=b(t)$, $H(s,0)=x$ and $H(s,1)=y$ for all $s,t$, such that $t\mapsto H(s,t)$ is a leafwise path for every $s$. Leafwise homotopy relative to endpoints is an equivalence relation, and homotopic relative endpoints means equivalent in this relation. Continuity is in $M$; the leaf topology is not used.
entry.strategy: Unpack the published relative-homotopy vocabulary on the square $I^2$ and the published notion of leaf. The only new clause is that every time-slice lies in a single leaf, which is what makes transverse transport well defined. Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are inherited from the published homotopy equivalence-relation results by keeping the leafwise condition at every stage; no topology finer than the topology of $M$ is introduced. The definition is choice-free.

entry.title: Germs of local diffeomorphisms at a point
entry.statement: Let $M,N$ be smooth manifolds and $x\in M$, $y\in N$. A **germ of local diffeomorphisms from $(M,x)$ to $(N,y)$** is an equivalence class of local diffeomorphisms $f:U\to V$ with $U$ open in $M$, $x\in U$, $V$ open in $N$, $y\in V$ and $f(x)=y$, two such being equivalent when they agree on some neighbourhood of $x$. When $M=N$ and $x=y$, write $\operatorname{Diff}_x(M)$ for the set of germs of local diffeomorphisms $(M,x)\to(M,x)$; composition of representatives makes $\operatorname{Diff}_x(M)$ a group, with identity the germ of $\mathrm{id}_M$ and inverse the germ of a local inverse.
entry.strategy: The germ relation follows the published germ-of-smooth-maps pattern, restricted to local diffeomorphisms. Composition and inversion of representatives are well defined on germs and satisfy the group laws; this is proved as the next lemma, which is recorded as the well-definedness certificate (`justified_by`) of this definition. No choice principle is used.

entry.title: Germs of local diffeomorphisms at a point form a group
entry.statement: With the notation of the preceding definition: composition of representatives induces a well-defined binary operation on $\operatorname{Diff}_x(M)$; this operation is associative, the germ of the identity is a two-sided identity, and every germ has a two-sided inverse. Hence $\operatorname{Diff}_x(M)$ is a group.
entry.strategy: Well-definedness: if $f\sim f'$ and $g\sim g'$ as germs at $x$ with composable targets, restrict all four maps to a common neighbourhood of $x$ on which $f=f'$ and $g=g'$; then $f\circ g=f'\circ g'$ near $x$. Associativity is inherited from composition of maps on a common neighbourhood. Identity and inverses: the germ of $\mathrm{id}_M$, and for a local diffeomorphism $f$ the germ of its local inverse, which exists by the definition of a local diffeomorphism and the inverse function theorem. The group axioms are then checked on representatives; the source records exactly this statement.

entry.title: A leafwise path determines a germ of a transverse diffeomorphism
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation of $M$, let $a$ be a leafwise path from $x$ to $y$, let $T$ be a local transversal to $F$ at $x$ and $T'$ a local transversal at $y$. Suppose $0=t_0<\dots<t_N=1$ and foliation charts $U_1,\dots,U_N$ satisfy $a([t_{i-1},t_i])\subseteq U_i$, and choose local transversals $T_i$ at $a(t_i)$ with $T_0=T$ and $T_N=T'$. Then the chart-wise transports along plaques compose to a germ of a local diffeomorphism $h_a:(T,x)\to(T',y)$, the **holonomy germ of $a$** along the displayed data. Every leafwise path admits such a finite chart chain, so every leafwise path together with the endpoint transversals determines at least one such germ.
entry.strategy: Compactness of $[0,1]$ and continuity of $a$ produce a finite chain of foliation charts. In a chart the plaques are the level sets of the transverse coordinates; the transport from $T_{i-1}$ to $T_i$ within $U_i$ keeps the transverse coordinates fixed and is a local diffeomorphism germ, because a transversal meets each nearby plaque in exactly one nearby point (transversality gives an invertible graph description, so the smooth inverse function theorem applies). Consecutive charts describe the same plaque germ through their common point by the published compatible-germs lemma, so the transports compose. The displayed auxiliary choices are recorded; their independence is the next lemma.

entry.title: The holonomy germ is independent of the foliation chart chain
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. In the situation of the preceding lemma, the germ $h_a:(T,x)\to(T',y)$ depends only on the leafwise path $a$ and the endpoint transversals $T,T'$: it is unchanged by passing to a refinement of the chart chain, by changing the subdivision points, and by changing the auxiliary intermediate transversals $T_1,\dots,T_{N-1}$. Consequently $h_a=h_a(T',T)$ is a well-defined germ of a local diffeomorphism $(T,x)\to(T',y)$.
entry.strategy: Two chains admit a common refinement by taking foliation charts through each point of the path and intersecting covers; along a common subinterval the plaque transports agree because overlapping plaques through a common point determine the same germ. Changing an intermediate transversal $T_i$ replaces the pair of consecutive transports by an equivalent composite: all maps involved keep the transverse coordinates of one common chart fixed, and composing the two descriptions gives the identity on a common neighbourhood. Both reductions are finite and local, and repeated comparison proves the assertion.

entry.title: Holonomy depends only on leafwise homotopy relative to endpoints
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation of $M$, let $a,b$ be leafwise paths from $x$ to $y$ that are leafwise homotopic relative to endpoints, and let $T,T'$ be local transversals at $x$ and $y$. Then $h_a(T',T)=h_b(T',T)$ as germs. In particular the holonomy germ of a leafwise path depends only on its leafwise homotopy class relative to endpoints and on the endpoint transversals.
entry.strategy: Subdivide the unit square into finitely many small rectangles each mapped by the homotopy into a single foliation chart: continuity on the compact square gives a uniform subdivision. In one chart, replace the homotopy on a rectangle by its two boundary paths; the two boundary paths from the same point to the same point differ only within one plaque, and the coordinate computation shows that they induce the same plaque transport. Chaining these replacements over the finitely many rectangles replaces $a$ by $b$ step by step, and the chain-independence lemma makes each replacement leave the endpoint germ unchanged. Hence $h_a=h_b$.

entry.title: Holonomy respects path concatenation and reversal
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $a$ be a leafwise path from $x$ to $y$, let $b$ be a leafwise path from $y$ to $z$, and let $T,S,R$ be local transversals at $x,y,z$. Then, with $a*b$ the concatenation (traverse $a$, then $b$), $h_{a*b}(R,T)=h_b(R,S)\circ h_a(S,T)$. Also $h_{a^{-1}}(T,S)=\bigl(h_a(S,T)\bigr)^{-1}$, where $a^{-1}$ is the reversed leafwise path.
entry.strategy: Verify first in a single foliation chart: concatenating two paths contained in one chart composes the plaque transports, and reversing a path inverts the local diffeomorphism, because the plaque transport within a chart is the same map read in the two directions. The general case follows by refining a chart chain for $a*b$ so that it contains chains for $a$ and $b$ meeting at the middle transversal $S$, and then applying the chain-independence lemma; inverses of germs exist by the germ-group lemma.

entry.title: The holonomy representation and the holonomy group of a leaf
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation of $M$, $L$ a leaf, $x\in L$, and $T$ a local transversal to $F$ at $x$. By the germ-group lemma the germs at $x$ of local diffeomorphisms of $T$ form a group $\operatorname{Diff}_x(T)$. Define the **holonomy representation of $L$ at $x$** (relative to $T$) by $$\rho_x:\pi_1(L,x)\to\operatorname{Diff}_x(T),\qquad \rho_x([a]):=h_a(T,T),$$ the germ of the transverse transport of $T$ along the leaf loop $a$. Homotopy invariance makes $\rho_x$ well defined on classes and multiplicativity makes it a homomorphism. The **holonomy group** of $L$ at $x$ is $\operatorname{Hol}(L,x):=\rho_x(\pi_1(L,x))\le\operatorname{Diff}_x(T)$. Replacing $T$ by another local transversal at $x$ replaces $\rho_x$ by a conjugate homomorphism (the conjugating germ is the plaque transport between the two transversals at $x$), so the kernel of $\rho_x$ and the conjugacy class of the holonomy group do not depend on the choice of $T$.
entry.strategy: The definitions assemble the previous items: the germ-group structure, the holonomy germ of a path, homotopy invariance for well-definedness, and concatenation for multiplicativity. The change-of-transversal formula is the associativity of plaque transports at a point, as recorded in the source's property 3 of the holonomy maps; it makes the kernel and the conjugacy class intrinsic while leaving the representative $\rho_x$ transversal-dependent. No choice beyond the standing $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

entry.title: The deck group of a connected covering acts by a covering-space action
entry.statement: Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering map with connected total space $E$. Then the deck group $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ acts on $E$ by a covering-space action: every $e\in E$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ with $hU\cap U=\varnothing$ for every nonidentity $h\in\operatorname{Deck}(p)$.
entry.strategy: Take an evenly covered neighbourhood $W$ of $p(e)$ and let $U$ be the sheet of $p^{-1}(W)$ containing $e$. Every deck transformation maps sheets over $W$ onto sheets over $W$. If $hU=U$, then $h$ carries the unique point of $U$ over $p(e)$ to itself, so $h=\mathrm{id}$ by one-point determination on the connected total space. Hence for $h\ne\mathrm{id}$ the sheets $hU$ and $U$ are distinct, and distinct sheets over $W$ are disjoint. Thus $hU\cap U=\varnothing$.

entry.title: The covering of a leaf associated with the holonomy kernel exists
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation, $L$ a leaf with base point $x$, $T$ a local transversal at $x$, $\rho_x:\pi_1(L,x)\to\operatorname{Diff}_x(T)$ the holonomy representation and $K=\ker\rho_x$. Then there is a connected covering $p:\widehat L\to L$ with $p_*\pi_1(\widehat L,\hat x)=K$ for a point $\hat x$ over $x$: take the universal cover $\widetilde L\to L$, identify $\pi_1(L,x)$ with its deck group, and put $\widehat L:=\widetilde L/K$. Moreover any two connected coverings of $L$ with image subgroup $K$ are isomorphic over $L$.
entry.strategy: The leaf $L$ carries its smooth manifold structure, so it is nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected (charts map to convex Euclidean sets), hence has a universal cover. The deck group of that cover is $\pi_1(L,x)$ and acts by a covering-space action; restricting to the subgroup $K$ keeps the covering-space property, so the orbit map $\widetilde L\to\widetilde L/K$ is a covering whose deck group is $K$ (the acting group), and $\widetilde L$ is simply connected, so $\pi_1(\widehat L)\cong K$ with image exactly $K$ under $p_*$. Uniqueness is the covering-space lifting criterion applied in both directions, using the universal cover's dominating property.

entry.title: The holonomy cover of a leaf
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation, $L$ a leaf with base point $x$, $T$ a local transversal at $x$, $\rho_x$ the holonomy representation and $K=\ker\rho_x$. The **holonomy cover** of $L$ (relative to $T$) is the connected covering $p:\widehat L\to L$ with $p_*\pi_1(\widehat L,\hat x)=K$ supplied by the preceding lemma, equipped with a base point $\hat x$ over $x$; it is unique up to a unique isomorphism over $L$. By construction $\pi_1(\widehat L,\hat x)\cong K$ and $p$ is a covering of $L$ by the holonomy orbits of $\rho_x$.

The kernel is independent of the choice of $T$ because replacing $T$ conjugates $\rho_x$. This is the leaf-level input for the finite-holonomy normal model of the Reeb stability pair, which consumes the holonomy cover, not the universal cover.

entry.title: The monodromy groupoid of a foliation
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation of $M$. The **monodromy groupoid** $\operatorname{Mon}(F)$ is the groupoid with object set $M$ whose arrows from $x$ to $y$ are the leafwise homotopy classes relative to endpoints of leafwise paths from $x$ to $y$ (there is no arrow when $x,y$ lie in different leaves). Composition is induced by concatenation of leafwise paths, the identity at $x$ is the class of the constant path, and inverses are induced by path reversal. These operations are independent of representatives by the published homotopy results. The groupoid is set-theoretic: no topology is imposed and no smooth structure on the arrow set is asserted.
entry.strategy: The arrow set is the quotient of the set of leafwise paths by leafwise homotopy relative to endpoints, an equivalence relation by the preceding definition. Composition of classes is well defined because homotopies compose, associativity holds up to the standard reparametrisation homotopy, the constant path is a two-sided identity, and reversal is a leafwise path giving the inverse class. Only set-theoretic structure is claimed here; the smooth/étale structure is not constructed on this page.

entry.title: The holonomy groupoid of a foliation
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation of $M$. Two leafwise paths with the same endpoints are **holonomy-equivalent** when their holonomy germs relative to one, equivalently by chain independence every, choice of local transversals at the endpoints agree. The **holonomy groupoid** $\operatorname{Hol}(F)$ is the groupoid with object set $M$ whose arrows are the holonomy classes of leafwise paths, with composition induced by concatenation. It is the quotient of the monodromy groupoid by the relation that identifies arrows with equal holonomy germs; arrows whose endpoints are not composable have no composite. The projection $\operatorname{Mon}(F)\to\operatorname{Hol}(F)$ sends a homotopy class to its holonomy class.
entry.strategy: The relation refines leafwise homotopy relative to endpoints (homotopic paths have equal germs) and is independent of the phrase 'one, equivalently every' by chain independence. Composition of holonomy classes is well defined by multiplicativity of holonomy germs; the well-definedness of the quotient structure is proved as the next lemma, which is recorded as this definition's `justified_by` certificate. As with the monodromy groupoid, no topology on the arrow set is asserted here.

entry.title: Holonomy classes form a groupoid congruence
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. On the set of leafwise paths of $F$, the relation 'same endpoints and equal holonomy germs' is an equivalence relation refining leafwise homotopy relative to endpoints, and it is a congruence for concatenation: if $a,a'$ and $b,b'$ satisfy $a\sim a'$ and $b\sim b'$, and $b*a$ and $b'*a'$ are defined, then $b*a\sim b'*a'$. Consequently the quotient $\operatorname{Hol}(F)$ is a groupoid and the projection $\operatorname{Mon}(F)\to\operatorname{Hol}(F)$ is a groupoid morphism.
entry.strategy: The relation is an equivalence relation because equality of germs is, and it refines leafwise homotopy by homotopy invariance of holonomy. For the congruence: by multiplicativity, $h_{b*a}=h_b\circ h_a$ and $h_{b'*a'}=h_{b'}\circ h_{a'}$; equal germs have the same endpoints and compose to equal germs by the germ-group lemma, so $b*a\sim b'*a'$. Identities and inverses are compatible for the same reason, giving the groupoid structure on the quotient.

entry.title: The isotropy of the holonomy groupoid is the leaf holonomy group
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation, $x\in M$, $L$ the leaf through $x$, $T$ a local transversal at $x$ and $\rho_x:\pi_1(L,x)\to\operatorname{Diff}_x(T)$ the holonomy representation. Then the isotropy group $\operatorname{Hol}(F)(x,x)$ of the holonomy groupoid is canonically isomorphic to the holonomy group $\operatorname{Hol}(L,x)=\rho_x(\pi_1(L,x))$: the map sending the holonomy class of a leaf loop at $x$ to its holonomy germ is a group isomorphism. In particular the isotropy is trivial if and only if the holonomy representation is trivial.
entry.strategy: Arrows $x\to x$ of $\operatorname{Hol}(F)$ are holonomy classes of leaf loops at $x$; by definition of the relation they are in bijection with their germs, and the germ of a loop is $\rho_x([a])$, so the map is a bijection onto $\rho_x(\pi_1(L,x))$. Multiplicativity of holonomy germs makes it a homomorphism: the class of the concatenation $a*b$ maps to $h_b\circ h_a$, which is the product of the images. Hence it is an isomorphism of groups, and vanishing of the image is equivalent to triviality of the representation.

entry.title: Smooth maps transverse to a regular foliation
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation of $M$ with tangent distribution $D=TF$, let $N$ be a smooth manifold and $f:N\to M$ a smooth map. Then $f$ is **transverse to $F$ at $x\in N$** when $$df_x(T_xN)+D_{f(x)}=T_{f(x)}M,$$ and **transverse to $F$** when this holds at every $x\in N$. When $N\subseteq M$ and $f$ is the inclusion this is transversality of a submanifold to $F$; the condition forces $\dim N\ge\operatorname{codim}F$ at every point, and it is automatic when $\operatorname{codim}F=0$.
entry.strategy: Specialise the published definition of transverse smooth maps to the case where the second map is the inclusion of the leaf distribution $D$, viewed as a smooth subbundle of $TM$ along the base map. All clauses are pointwise linear algebra in the tangent spaces, so the definition inherits the conventions of the published transversality vocabulary and adds no choice beyond the standing $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

entry.title: The pullback foliation under a transverse map
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F$ be a regular foliation of $M$ of codimension $q$, let $N$ be a smooth manifold and $f:N\to M$ a smooth map transverse to $F$. Put $D_x^*:=(df_x)^{-1}\bigl(D_{f(x)}\bigr)$, where $D=TF$. Then $D^*$ is a smooth rank-$(\dim N-q)$ distribution on $N$, it is integrable, and the associated regular foliation $f^*F$ has as its leaves the connected components of the preimages $f^{-1}(L)$ of the leaves $L$ of $F$. Each leaf of $f^*F$ is mapped by $f$ into a leaf of $F$.
entry.strategy: In a foliation chart on $M$, let $y:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be the transverse-coordinate submersion, so $D|_U=\ker dy$. Transversality implies $g=y\circ f$ is a submersion on $f^{-1}(U)$, because the induced map $T_xN\to T_{f(x)}M/D_{f(x)}$ is surjective. Thus $D_x^*=\ker dg_x$ has constant rank $\dim N-q$, and the constant-rank kernel theorem makes it a smooth subbundle. Submersion coordinates give local integral plaques as connected level sets of $g$, proving integrability directly without extending arbitrary sections along a possibly noninjective $f$ to ambient vector fields. On overlaps these plaques agree because they are precisely the local connected preimages of the original plaques; the foliation/distribution correspondence supplies the associated regular foliation. A connected leaf preimage, equipped with its pulled-back plaque topology, is assembled from these plaques; every connected integral manifold maps into a single leaf and conversely each such connected component is an integral manifold. Maximality therefore gives exactly the asserted leaves. The pullback and quotient bundle constructions identify the same kernel as $TN\to f^*TM\to f^*(TM/D)$. Only the standing $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used.

entry.title: The quotient foliation under a free and properly discontinuous foliated action
entry.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\Gamma$ be a group acting on a connected smooth manifold $M$ by diffeomorphisms, and suppose the action is **free and properly discontinuous**: $\gamma\cdot x=x$ implies $\gamma=e$ for all $x\in M$, and for every compact $K\subseteq M$ the set $\{\gamma\in\Gamma:\gamma K\cap K\neq\varnothing\}$ is finite. Let $F$ be a regular foliation of $M$ preserved by $\Gamma$, so every $\gamma$ maps leaves onto leaves, with tangent distribution $D=TF$. Then: (1) $M/\Gamma$ carries a unique smooth structure for which the orbit map $\pi:M\to M/\Gamma$ is a local diffeomorphism, and with this structure $\pi$ is a covering map; (2) there is a unique regular foliation $F/\Gamma$ on $M/\Gamma$ whose leaves are the images $\pi(L)$ of the leaves of $F$, and its codimension equals $\operatorname{codim}F$; (3) the tangent distribution of $F/\Gamma$ is $d\pi(D)$.
entry.strategy: Proper discontinuity gives at each point a neighbourhood meeting none of its nonidentity translates, so the orbit map is a covering and the action is a covering-space action. Hausdorff and second countability follow from the closed orbit relation: for compact $K$ only finitely many $\gamma$ satisfy $\gamma K\cap K\neq\varnothing$, and distinct orbits are separated by invariant open sets built from finitely many such $\gamma$. Smooth structure: charts of $M$ composed with local inverses of $\pi$; two local sections over a common connected open set differ there by a single group element, so transitions are smooth restrictions and the atlas is well defined; uniqueness follows because any smooth structure making $\pi$ a local diffeomorphism is compatible with this atlas. Foliation: the pushforward distribution $d\pi(D)$ is well defined, smooth of rank $\dim M-\operatorname{codim}F$ and integrable, and its maximal integral manifolds are exactly the images $\pi(L)$ of the leaves; this gives the unique regular foliation $F/\Gamma$ with the stated codimension.

entry.title: The suspension foliation of a representation of the fundamental group
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $B$ be a connected smooth manifold with base point $b_0$, let $F$ be a smooth manifold, let $p:\widetilde B\to B$ be a universal cover and let $\rho:\pi_1(B,b_0)\to\operatorname{Diff}(F)$ be a homomorphism into the diffeomorphism group of $F$. Using the isomorphism $\pi_1(B,b_0)\cong\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde B\to B)$, let $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ act on $\widetilde B\times F$ diagonally by $$\gamma\cdot(x,y):=\bigl(\gamma\cdot x,\rho(\gamma)(y)\bigr).$$ This is a covering-space action by diffeomorphisms, so the quotient $M_\rho:=(\widetilde B\times F)/\pi_1(B,b_0)$ is a smooth manifold, the orbit map $\pi$ is a covering, and the product foliation of $\widetilde B\times F$ by the leaves $\widetilde B\times\{y\}$, which is invariant under the action, descends by the quotient-foliation proposition to a regular foliation $F_\rho$ of $M_\rho$ of codimension $\dim F$, the **suspension foliation** of $\rho$.
entry.strategy: Verify the covering-space action: given $(x,y)$, choose $U\subseteq\widetilde B$ with $\gamma U\cap U=\varnothing$ for all nonidentity $\gamma$ (the deck action of a universal cover is such an action by the deck-group lemma), then $(U\times F)\cap\gamma(U\times F)=\varnothing$ because the first coordinate already separates. Freeness is clear from $\gamma x=x$. The product foliation is invariant because $\gamma\cdot(\widetilde B\times\{y\})=\widetilde B\times\{\rho(\gamma)y\}$. Apply the quotient-foliation proposition to obtain the manifold, the covering orbit map and the descended foliation. This is the standard suspension of a flat bundle construction; no topology on the arrow set of a groupoid is involved.

entry.title: Suspension holonomy is the germ of the represented monodromy action
entry.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. In the suspension of the representation $\rho$ let $\gamma:[0,1]\to B$ be a loop at $b_0$ with class $[\gamma]\in\pi_1(B,b_0)$, let $\tilde x\in\widetilde B$ lie over $b_0$, let $\tilde x_\gamma$ be the lift of $\gamma$ with $\tilde x_\gamma(0)=\tilde x$, so $\tilde x_\gamma(1)=[\gamma]\cdot\tilde x$, and let $y\in F$. Then $a(t):=\pi(\tilde x_\gamma(t),y)$ is a leafwise path of $F_\rho$, and its holonomy germ between the local transversals $T=\pi(\{\tilde x\}\times F)$ at the start and the corresponding slice at the end is the germ at $y$ of $\rho([\gamma])^{-1}$: $$h_a=\text{germ}_y\bigl(\rho([\gamma])^{-1}\bigr).$$ Moreover the leaf $L_y=\pi(\widetilde B\times\{y\})$ is diffeomorphic to $\widetilde B/K_y$ with $K_y=\{\gamma:\rho(\gamma)y=y\}$, and under $\pi_1(L_y)\cong K_y$ the holonomy representation of the leaf is $\gamma\mapsto\rho(\gamma)^{-1}$.
entry.strategy: Work on $\widetilde B\times F$, where the product foliation has the straight leaves $\widetilde B\times\{y\}$; the slice $\{\tilde x\}\times F$ is a local transversal because $\pi$ is a covering and the two directions are complementary. Transporting the slice along $t\mapsto(\tilde x_\gamma(t),y)$ keeps the $F$-coordinate, so at $t=1$ the point $(\tilde x_\gamma(1),y)=(\gamma\cdot\tilde x,y)$ is identified in $M_\rho$ with $(\tilde x,\rho(\gamma)^{-1}y)$; hence the germ is $\rho([\gamma])^{-1}$ (with the action convention displayed). For the leaf: $\pi$ restricts to a bijection $\widetilde B/K_y\to L_y$ that is a local diffeomorphism, and $K_y$ acts as a covering-space action, so $\pi_1(L_y)\cong K_y$ by the deck-group theorem; the same transport computation gives the restriction of $\rho(\,\cdot\,)^{-1}$.

entry.title: Holonomy is a germ, not a globally defined return map
entry.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The holonomy of a leafwise path is a germ of a local diffeomorphism between local transversals, not a globally defined return map: a representative is defined only on some open neighbourhood of the base point in the transversal, and different representatives of the same germ may differ arbitrarily far from that point. The Poincaré return map of a periodic orbit of a flow is the special case in which the first-return construction defines a map on a fixed section; that is additional structure, not part of the general definition. Statements about 'the' return map along a leaf loop must therefore be read as statements about the holonomy germ.
entry.strategy: Point at the construction and its certificates: the finite chain in the construction of the germ is defined on a neighbourhood of the base point only, and chain independence compares germs, so nothing defines values away from the base point. The source's presentation starts from the Poincaré return map as motivation and then replaces it by germs precisely because the return map requires a chosen section and a first-return time. No proof obligation beyond the cited construction items.

entry.title: Holonomy and monodromy groupoids need not be Hausdorff
entry.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The monodromy groupoid and the holonomy groupoid of a foliation carry smooth structures making them étale Lie groupoids, and they can fail to be Hausdorff even though the foliated manifold is Hausdorff; the two failures are independent, in the sense that either groupoid can be Hausdorff while the other is not. This item records the phenomenon; it is not proved here, and no topology on the groupoid arrow sets is constructed on this page. The groupoid definitions of this page are set-theoretic and make no Hausdorffness assertion.
entry.strategy: Recorded, not proved here. The phenomenon is stated in the sources, which also give a mechanism: a non-contractible loop in a leaf approached by contractible loops in nearby leaves makes elements of the monodromy groupoid converge both to a nontrivial arrow and to a unit, which is incompatible with Hausdorffness. A self-contained example (Reeb foliation of the three-sphere; the foliation of the complement of the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$ by the fibres of a projection) would require constructing the étale topology on the arrow set, which this page deliberately does not do; the recorded statement suffices for the design's purpose of preventing a silent Hausdorffness assumption.

entry.title: The Kronecker foliation of the torus has dense leaves and trivial leaf holonomy
entry.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\alpha\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$ and let $F_\alpha$ be the linear foliation of $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ whose leaves are the images of the lines $t\mapsto[p+t(1,\alpha)]$. Then every leaf is dense in $\mathbb T^2$, every leaf is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R$, and the holonomy group of every point is trivial: for every leaf $L$ and $x\in L$ the holonomy representation $\rho_x:\pi_1(L,x)\to\operatorname{Diff}_x(T)$ has trivial domain $\pi_1(L,x)=0$, so every leaf loop has the identity holonomy germ. In particular this foliation has dense leaves while its holonomy is as trivial as that of a product foliation.
entry.strategy: Density: it suffices to treat the leaf through $[0]$. The fractional parts of the multiples of $\alpha$ form a dense subgroup of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$: for $\varepsilon>0$ the pigeonhole principle applied to $0,\alpha,\dots,N\alpha$ with $1/N<\varepsilon$ produces $\beta=k\alpha$ with $0<\beta<\varepsilon$ in the circle, and the multiples of $\beta$ form an $\varepsilon$-net; then for any target $(u,v)$ choose $t=u+mk$ with $m\beta$ close to $v-\alpha u$. Every other leaf is a translate, and translations are homeomorphisms, so all leaves are dense. Leaf structure: $t\mapsto[(t,\alpha t)]$ is a continuous bijection onto the leaf (injectivity uses irrationality of $\alpha$) and an injective immersion; in flow-box coordinates of the linear foliation it is a straight-line graph, hence a local diffeomorphism onto the leaf with its leaf structure, so by uniqueness of the maximal integral manifold structure the leaf is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R$. Hence $\pi_1(L,x)=0$ because $\mathbb R$ is convex, and the holonomy representation is trivial; homotopy invariance identifies every leaf-loop germ with the identity germ.

entry.title: The Möbius band's central leaf has reflection holonomy
entry.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\mathrm{Mob}=(\mathbb R\times(-1,1))/\mathbb Z$ be the smooth Möbius band, with the action $k\cdot(t,x)=(t+k,(-1)^kx)$, and let $F$ be the foliation whose leaves are the images of the horizontal segments $\mathbb R\times\{x\}$; the projection $[t,x]\mapsto[t]$ is a circle bundle to which $F$ is transverse. Then the middle leaf $L_{\mathrm{mid}}=\pi(\mathbb R\times\{0\})$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1$ and its holonomy group at every point is $\mathbb Z/2$: the generator of $\pi_1(L_{\mathrm{mid}})\cong\mathbb Z$ has holonomy germ the reflection $x\mapsto-x$ of the transversal, and its square has trivial germ. Every other leaf is diffeomorphic to $S^1$ (it wraps twice around the band) and has trivial holonomy group.
entry.strategy: The band is the suspension of the representation $\rho:\mathbb Z\to\operatorname{Diff}((-1,1))$, $k\mapsto(x\mapsto(-1)^kx)$, over $B=S^1$, so the suspension proposition applies: the leaf through $(0,0)$ is the image of $\mathbb R\times\{0\}$, and the base loop $\gamma$ of $S^1$ has leaf path from $[0,0]$ to $[1,0]=[0,0]$ whose holonomy germ is $\rho(1)^{-1}:x\mapsto-x$, a nontrivial involution; the isotropy proposition identifies the holonomy group with the cyclic group generated by this germ, of order $2$. For $x\ne0$ the stabilizer of $x$ under the action is $2\mathbb Z$, so the corresponding leaf is $\mathbb R/2\mathbb Z\cong S^1$ and the class generating its fundamental group is the double of the core loop, whose holonomy germ is $\rho(2)^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$; hence the holonomy group is trivial.

entry.title: The suspension of a circle diffeomorphism: leaves and return germs
entry.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f:S^1\to S^1$ be a diffeomorphism and let $M_f=(\mathbb R\times S^1)/\mathbb Z$ with $k\cdot(t,y)=(t+k,f^k(y))$; let $F_f$ be the suspension foliation of the representation $\rho(k)=f^k$ over $B=S^1$. Then: (i) the leaf $L_y$ through $[0,y]$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1$ when the orbit of $y$ under $f$ is periodic, and to $\mathbb R$ otherwise; (ii) if $y$ has minimal period $k\ge1$, the leaf loop $a(t)=[(t,y)]$, $t\in[0,k]$, generates $\pi_1(L_y)\cong\mathbb Z$ and has holonomy germ at $[0,y]$ equal to the germ of $f^{-k}$ at $y$, so the holonomy group of $L_y$ is the cyclic group generated by that germ; (iii) in particular for $f$ the identity the foliation is the product foliation of $\mathbb T^2$ by circles and all holonomy germs are trivial, while for a rotation by $2\pi p/q$ every leaf is a circle and every holonomy germ is trivial.
entry.strategy: (i) $\pi$ restricted to $\mathbb R\times\{y\}$ factors through the period group $K_y=\{k:f^k(y)=y\}$ and is a diffeomorphism onto $L_y$ with $\mathbb R/K_y$, which is $S^1$ for a nontrivial period group and $\mathbb R$ otherwise. (ii) The path $a$ is closed exactly when $f^k(y)=y$; the suspension-holonomy proposition gives the germ $\rho(k)^{-1}=f^{-k}$ at $y$, and the isotropy proposition identifies the holonomy group of the leaf with the image of its fundamental group, which is generated by this class. (iii) For $f=\mathrm{id}$ the total space is $\mathbb T^2$ with the product foliation and every $K_y=\mathbb Z$ acts trivially on the fibre, so all germs are trivial; for a rotation of order $q$, $f^q=\mathrm{id}$ and the generator has trivial germ.

entry.title: The flat-bundle foliation from a linear representation
entry.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $A\in\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb R)$ and let $M_A=(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n)/\mathbb Z$ with $k\cdot(t,v)=(t+k,A^kv)$, a suspension of the linear representation $\rho(k)=A^k$ over $B=S^1$; let $F_A$ be the suspension foliation of $M_A$. Then: (i) $M_A\to S^1$, $[t,v]\mapsto[t]$, is a smooth fibre bundle with fibre $\mathbb R^n$ and locally constant transition functions (a flat vector bundle); (ii) if $Av=v$, then the leaf through $[0,v]$ is a circle and the leaf loop $a(t)=[(t,v)]$, $t\in[0,1]$, has holonomy germ the germ of $A^{-1}$ at $v$; for $A$ diagonal with all eigenvalues different from $1$, the leaf through the origin is a circle whose holonomy group is generated by the germ of $A^{-1}$ at $0$ and is nontrivial whenever $A\ne I$; (iii) the foliation $F_A$ is transverse to the fibres of the bundle projection.
entry.strategy: (i) Use the two standard charts of $S^1$ and the trivializations $[t,v]\mapsto([t],v)$ over each chart; on the overlap the change of coordinates is the locally constant map $v\mapsto A^{\pm1}v$, so $M_A$ is a flat fibre bundle over the circle. (ii) The leaf through $[0,v]$ is the image of $\mathbb R\times\{v\}$; it is a circle when $Av=v$, and the suspension-holonomy proposition computes the holonomy of the closed leaf path as the germ of $\rho(1)^{-1}=A^{-1}$; the isotropy proposition turns that germ into the holonomy group of the leaf. (iii) The leaf directions are the $\mathbb R$ directions and the fibre directions are the $\mathbb R^n$ directions, which are complementary and of the correct dimensions, so transversality is a pointwise linear fact at every $[t,v]$.

entry.title: A nontransverse pullback need not reproduce the rank of a foliation
entry.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The following inference is false: for an arbitrary smooth map $f:N\to M$ and a regular foliation $F$ of $M$, the inverse-image spaces $D_t^*:=(df_t)^{-1}(T_{f(t)}F)$ form a smooth distribution of constant rank $\dim N-\operatorname{codim}F$ and define a regular pullback foliation whose leaves are the connected components of leaf preimages. Counterexample: let $M=\mathbb R^2$ with the horizontal foliation, $N=\mathbb R$, and $f(t)=(0,t^2)$. Since $df_t(v)=(0,2tv)$ and $T_{f(t)}F=\mathbb R\times\{0\}$, one has $D_t^*=\{0\}$ for $t\ne0$ but $D_0^*=T_0\mathbb R$. Thus the rank jumps from $0$ to $1$ at $0$, so $D^*$ is not a regular distribution. The map is transverse to $F$ for $t\ne0$ and nontransverse at $0$. This refutes the rank and regular-distribution inference without the transversality hypothesis.
entry.strategy: Use the inverse-image convention of [[prop-pullback-foliation-under-a-transverse-map]]: $D_t^*$ consists of tangent vectors $v$ such that $df_t(v)$ lies in the horizontal line. For $f(t)=(0,t^2)$, this condition is $2tv=0$. If $t\ne0$ it forces $v=0$, whereas at $t=0$ every tangent vector qualifies. Hence rank is nonconstant and the inverse-image spaces cannot form a smooth vector subbundle of $T\mathbb R$. For $t\ne0$ the vertical image of $df_t$ and the horizontal leaf tangent span $\mathbb R^2$; at $0$ their sum is only the horizontal line. The horizontal-leaf preimages are finite sets, so their connected components are points; their zero-dimensional decomposition cannot have the displayed rank-jumping tangent spaces. The construction uses no choice beyond the standing foliation-interface premise.

entry.title: Two nonhomotopic leaf loops can have the same holonomy germ
entry.statement:
Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). The
following inference is false: two leaf loops with the same holonomy germ are
leafwise homotopic relative to endpoints, so that the holonomy groupoid would
coincide with the monodromy groupoid.

**Counterexample.** In the Möbius band foliation constructed below, the middle leaf has
$\pi_1(L_{\mathrm{mid}})\cong\mathbb Z$ generated by the core loop $\gamma$,
whose holonomy germ is the reflection $x\mapsto-x$. The double $2\gamma$ is not
null-homotopic in the leaf, yet its holonomy germ is the square of the
reflection, that is, the identity germ, as is the germ of the constant loop.
Hence the constant loop and $2\gamma$ are nonhomotopic relative to endpoints and
have the same holonomy germ, and the kernel of the holonomy representation is
the nontrivial subgroup $2\mathbb Z\le\mathbb Z$; the natural map
$\operatorname{Mon}(F)\to\operatorname{Hol}(F)$ is not injective in general.
entry.strategy: Use the previous example: multiplicativity of holonomy germs gives $h_{2\gamma}=h_\gamma\circ h_\gamma=r\circ r=\mathrm{id}$, while $2\gamma\ne 0$ in $\pi_1(L_{\mathrm{mid}})\cong\mathbb Z$; the constant loop has identity germ and is null-homotopic. The two loops therefore have equal germs and unequal classes, so the stated inference fails and the two groupoids are genuinely different quotients of the path groupoid.

entry.title: C¹ germs of local diffeomorphisms at a point
entry.statement:
Let $T$ be a one-dimensional manifold equipped with a $C^1$ atlas: its charts
are homeomorphisms onto open subsets of $\mathbb R$ whose transition maps are
$C^1$ with $C^1$ inverses, and "of class $C^1$" for maps of $T$ means of class
$C^1$ in these charts, which is exactly the Euclidean notion of
[[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Fix $x\in T$.

A **$C^1$ local diffeomorphism of $T$ at $x$ fixing $x$** is a map
$f:U\to T$ defined on an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq T$ of $x$ such that
$f(U)$ is open, $f:U\to f(U)$ is a bijection, $f(x)=x$, and both $f$ and
$f^{-1}:f(U)\to U$ are of class $C^1$. Two such local diffeomorphisms
$f:U\to T$ and $g:V\to T$ define the same **$C^1$ germ at $x$** when they agree
on some neighbourhood of $x$ contained in $U\cap V$; write $f\sim_x g$ for this
relation.

The equivalence classes of $\sim_x$ are the **$C^1$ germs of local
diffeomorphisms of $T$ at $x$**, and their set is denoted
$\operatorname{Diff}^1_x(T)$. Composition of representatives induces a binary
operation
$$\operatorname{Diff}^1_x(T)\times\operatorname{Diff}^1_x(T)\to\operatorname{Diff}^1_x(T),$$
the class of $f\circ g$ being independent of the chosen representatives, and
with this operation $\operatorname{Diff}^1_x(T)$ is a group ([[def-group]])
whose identity is the germ of $\mathrm{id}_T$. Well-definedness of the
operation, associativity, the two-sided identity and two-sided inverses are
verified in [[lem-c1-germs-of-local-diffeomorphisms-form-a-group]].

Finally suppose an orientation of a neighbourhood of $x$ is fixed, represented
by a chart $t$ at $x$ with $t(x)=0$; write $\tilde f$ for the coordinate
expression of a representative $f$. The sign of the derivative
$\tilde f'(0)$ is independent of the positively oriented chart and of the
representative of the germ, so the germs whose representatives have
$\tilde f'(0)>0$ in such a chart are well defined. They form a subgroup
$$\operatorname{Diff}^{1,+}_x(T)\le\operatorname{Diff}^1_x(T)$$
([[def-subgroup]]), the **orientation-preserving $C^1$ germs at $x$**; both the
invariance of the sign and the subgroup property are proved in
[[lem-c1-germs-of-local-diffeomorphisms-form-a-group]].

Only the case $\dim T=1$ is used in this pair, and there only for the transverse
coordinate of a codimension-one foliation, where the sign of the derivative is
the transverse orientation datum.
entry.strategy: The germ equivalence, composition, inverse and derivative-sign invariance are verified in [[lem-c1-germs-of-local-diffeomorphisms-form-a-group]]. The $C^1$ local-diffeomorphism and group/subgroup terminology use [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], [[def-group]] and [[def-subgroup]].

entry.title: C¹ codimension-one regular foliations and transverse orientation
entry.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). A **$C^1$
codimension-one foliation atlas** on $M$ is a family of charts
$$\varphi_\alpha=(x_\alpha,t_\alpha):U_\alpha\to\mathbb R^{n-1}\times\mathbb R,$$
with the $U_\alpha\subseteq M$ open covering $M$, each $\varphi_\alpha$ a
homeomorphism onto its image whose inverse is of class $C^1$ and whose
components are of class $C^1$ ([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]), such that
for every $\alpha,\beta$ with $U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\ne\varnothing$ the transition
map, wherever defined, has the form
$$(x_\beta,t_\beta)=\bigl(g_{\beta\alpha}(x_\alpha,t_\alpha),\,h_{\beta\alpha}(t_\alpha)\bigr),$$
where $g_{\beta\alpha}$ is of class $C^1$ and $h_{\beta\alpha}$ is a
one-dimensional $C^1$ local diffeomorphism of intervals
([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]). Thus the second coordinate of a chart
depends only on the old second coordinate, and charts change along the first
coordinates arbitrarily inside the slices of constant second coordinate.

Charts of such an atlas are **foliation charts**. For a foliation chart
$\varphi_\alpha$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ the set of points of $U_\alpha$ whose
second coordinate equals $c$ is a **slice**, and each of its connected
components is a **plaque** of the atlas. Two points of $M$ are said to be
**plaque-chain equivalent** when they can be joined by a finite chain
$P_0,\dots,P_k$ of plaques with $P_{i-1}\cap P_i\ne\varnothing$ for
$1\le i\le k$; this is an equivalence relation. Its equivalence classes are the
**leaves** of the atlas, and the leaf through a point $p$ is written $L_p$. A
**$C^1$ codimension-one foliation** $F$ of $M$ is the leaf decomposition
determined by one such atlas; by
[[lem-c1-foliated-atlas-preserves-plaque-equivalence-and-transverse-orientation]]
the plaques and the leaf decomposition are unchanged if the atlas is replaced
by any other $C^1$ foliation atlas on $M$ with the same slices, so that plaques
and leaves are attributes of $F$ and not of a chosen atlas.

The foliation $F$ is **transversely oriented**, or **co-oriented**, when the
transverse coordinates can be signed consistently. Concretely, $F$ is
transversely oriented when there is a foliation atlas for $M$ presenting $F$ in
which every transition germ $h_{\beta\alpha}$ is orientation-preserving:
$h_{\beta\alpha}'(t)>0$ at every $t$ in its domain, equivalently each
$h_{\beta\alpha}$ is increasing. The signed form of the condition allows one to
choose, for every chart of a foliation atlas, a locally constant sign
$\varepsilon_\alpha\in\{+,-\}$ and to replace the transverse coordinate
$t_\alpha$ by $\varepsilon_\alpha t_\alpha$; all transitions become increasing
precisely when, on every nonempty overlap, the two sign choices compensate the
sign of $h_{\beta\alpha}'$. The equivalence of these formulations, and the fact
that transverse orientability is likewise independent of the atlas, are proved in
[[lem-c1-foliated-atlas-preserves-plaque-equivalence-and-transverse-orientation]].

In a transversely oriented foliation the two sides of each plaque carry a
consistent sign, and the local transversals to the plaques are ordered in a
way respected by all plaque transports; this is the only use made of transverse
orientation in this pair. All foliations below are $C^1$ and regular in the
above sense.
entry.strategy: The chart changes and plaque-chain relation are verified in [[lem-c1-foliated-atlas-preserves-plaque-equivalence-and-transverse-orientation]]. The $C^1$-map and local-inverse terms use [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and the ambient chart convention uses [[def-smooth-manifold]]. This is a C¹ regularity specialization of the foliation-atlas definition; transverse orientation is exactly consistent orientation of the one-dimensional normal coordinate.

entry.title: The countable-choice principle used in the foliation pair
entry.statement:
The **countable choice principle** used throughout this pair, written
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the assertion:

> For every sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a
> function $c$ with domain $\mathbb N$ such that $c(n)\in A_n$ for every
> $n\in\mathbb N$.

Here "sequence" means a function on $\mathbb N$ ([[def-function]]) and "choice
function" is the notion of [[def-choice-function]]; thus the displayed
statement says that every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function.

This is the sequence formulation of countable choice. The equivalent
nonempty-product formulation, that $\prod_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n$ is nonempty for
every sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets, is verified in
[[lem-countable-choice-sequence-and-product-formulations-are-equivalent]]; that
lemma is recorded as the well-definedness certificate of the present
definition.

In this pair $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is a stated hypothesis of the foliation
theorems and of the items whose proof selects countably many plaque data. It is
not assumed where a proof does not use it, and the items that consume it state
the hypothesis explicitly.

This pair-local carrier is retained deliberately: it restates the published
[[def-countable-choice]] in exactly the sequence form consumed by the
foliation items, and the published definition supplies the same principle. The
retention and its cross-batch consequences are recorded in the Step-3 report
of this pair (finding F4).

entry.title: Saturated neighbourhoods of a leaf
entry.statement:
Let $F$ be a regular foliation of a smooth manifold $M$
([[def-regular-foliation-atlas]]) and let $L$ be a leaf of $F$
([[def-leaf-of-a-regular-foliation]]).

An open set $U\subseteq M$ is **saturated**, or **invariant**, for $F$ when it
is a union of leaves of $F$; equivalently, when for every $x\in U$ the whole
leaf of $F$ through $x$ is contained in $U$. The equivalence is immediate from
the definitions: a union of leaves has the pointwise property, and conversely
the set of leaves meeting $U$ covers $U$ by the pointwise property, so $U$ is
their union.

A **saturated neighbourhood of $L$** is a saturated open set $U\subseteq M$
with $L\subseteq U$. If $U$ is saturated then $F$ restricts to a regular
foliation of $U$: the plaques of $F$ that meet $U$ form a foliation atlas of the
open submanifold $U$ ([[def-regular-foliation-atlas]]), and the leaves of the
restriction are the connected components of the plaque partition of $U$, which
are exactly the leaves of $F$ that meet $U$ ([[def-leaf-of-a-regular-foliation]]).

The neighbourhood conclusion of Reeb stability below is stated as the
existence, for every neighbourhood $W$ of $L$ in $M$, of a saturated
neighbourhood $U\subseteq W$ of $L$; this property of $L$ is recorded
separately below as **stability** of the leaf.
entry.strategy: Unfold the published leaf vocabulary: a leaf is a maximal connected integral manifold, saturated just says $U$ is a union of such leaves, and the equivalence with the pointwise condition is immediate from maximality. Saturation makes $U\cup$-closed and open, and the restriction statement follows since the leaves of $F$ meeting $U$ are the connected components of the plaque partition of $U$. No choice principle is used.

Let $\varphi:G\to H$ be a group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]]). Then:

1. if $G$ is finitely generated ([[def-finitely-generated-group]]), then its

entry.title: Smooth foliations tangent to the boundary
entry.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $W$ be a smooth
$n$-manifold with boundary, with boundary charts modelled on the half-space
$\mathbb H^n=\mathbb R^{n-1}\times[0,\infty)$ and smooth structure as in
[[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]] and
[[def-topological-manifold-with-boundary]]; thus
$\partial W$ is a closed embedded smooth $(n-1)$-manifold
([[thm-the-boundary-is-a-closed-embedded-smooth-n-minus-one-manifold]]).

Fix $1\le q\le n$ and split $\mathbb H^n=\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb H^q$. A
**regular foliation of $W$ tangent to $\partial W$ of codimension $q$** is a
regular foliation atlas for the smooth structure of $W$
([[def-regular-foliation-atlas]]) whose charts are relatively open subsets of
$\mathbb H^n$ and whose transition maps are compatible with the standard
decomposition of $\mathbb H^n$ into the model plaques
$\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\{y\}$, $y\in\mathbb H^q$; that is, on every overlap the
coordinates of the second factor depend only on the second coordinates of the
first factor, exactly as for a foliation atlas on a boundaryless manifold, and
the plaque decomposition restricts to the half-space.

The model plaques meet $\partial\mathbb H^n=\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\partial
\mathbb H^q$ in the sets $\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\{y\}$ with
$y\in\partial\mathbb H^q$. Consequently, near a boundary point of $W$ the
leaves of $F$ are the intersections of the model plaques with the half-space;
the boundary $\partial W$ is a union of leaves of $F$, and each such
boundary leaf, being a plaque intersection with a hyperplane, inherits the
structure of a regular foliation of codimension $q-1$; the tangent distribution
$TF$ of the foliation ([[def-smooth-distribution-on-a-manifold]]) is tangent to
the boundary along $\partial W$ in the sense that $T_p\partial W$ contains
$D_p=TF_p$ for $p\in\partial W$, while $D_p$ is transverse to the normal
direction of the boundary. A leaf of the foliation restricted to the interior
$\operatorname{Int}W$ is a leaf of $F$, and it need not meet $\partial W$.

The pair uses this vocabulary only for $q=1$: the Reeb foliations of the solid
torus and its gluing are tangent to the boundary, and the boundary torus of a
Reeb component is a single leaf.
entry.strategy: Transfer the published atlas definition to the half-space model: a chart for $W$ is a relatively open subset of $\mathbb H^n$ together with a diffeomorphism onto its image, and the model decomposition of $\mathbb H^n$ restricts to a plaque decomposition on the interior and on the boundary hyperplane $\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\partial\mathbb H^q$, so the boundary is a union of leaves and carries its own regular foliation of leaf dimension $n-q$ and boundary codimension $(n-1)-(n-q)=q-1$. Consistency of the definitions is a local computation in half-space charts; the collar and boundary-submanifold items of the manifolds-with-boundary page supply the identification of $\partial W$ with a smooth manifold. No additional choice principle is used.

entry.title: Stable leaves
entry.statement:
Let $F$ be a regular foliation of a smooth manifold $M$
([[def-regular-foliation-atlas]]) and let $L$ be a leaf of $F$.

The leaf $L$ is **stable** when every open neighbourhood $W$ of $L$ in $M$
contains a saturated neighbourhood of $L$
([[def-saturated-neighbourhood-of-a-leaf]]); equivalently, when the saturated
neighbourhoods of $L$ form a fundamental system of neighbourhoods of $L$.

More generally, a subset $B\subseteq M$ is **stable in the sense of Reeb** when
for every open neighbourhood $W$ of $B$ there is an open neighbourhood
$W'\subseteq W$ of $B$ such that every leaf of $F$ meeting $W'$ is contained in
$W$. For a leaf $B=L$ this is equivalent to stability of $L$: if such a $W'$
exists, then its saturation
$U=\bigcup\{L' : L'\text{ a leaf and } L'\cap W'\neq\varnothing\}$ is open and saturated (each box carries an open set to its open plaque saturation, and finite plaque transport carries this property along every leaf), contains $L$, and satisfies $U\subseteq W$ by the property of $W'$,
so $U$ is a saturated neighbourhood of $L$ inside $W$; conversely a saturated
neighbourhood $U\subseteq W$ of $L$ is itself a neighbourhood $W'\subseteq W$ of
$L$ every leaf meeting which is contained in $U\subseteq W$.

Stability of a leaf is a neighbourhood property: it depends only on the germ of
the foliation along $L$, since both quantifiers involve neighbourhoods of $L$.
This is the property that the local and global Reeb stability theorems below
establish under their finiteness hypotheses.
entry.strategy: The equivalence is a two-line saturation argument: the saturation $\bigcup\{L' : L'\cap W'\neq\varnothing\}$ of the Reeb neighbourhood $W'$ is contained in $W$ by hypothesis and is saturated and open, so it is a saturated neighbourhood of $L$; conversely a saturated neighbourhood $U\subseteq W$ is itself a Reeb neighbourhood. The definition records exactly the conclusion used by the global stability theorem. No choice principle is used.

entry.title: Transversely oriented codimension-one foliations
entry.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair, thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds]]). Let $F$ be a regular
codimension-one foliation of a smooth manifold $M$
([[def-regular-foliation-atlas]]) with tangent distribution $D=TF$, a smooth
rank-$(n-1)$ subbundle of $TM$
([[def-smooth-distribution-on-a-manifold]]).

The foliation $F$ is **transversely oriented**, or **co-oriented**, when there
is a nowhere-vanishing smooth $1$-form $\omega$ on $M$ whose kernel is $D$:
$$D=\ker\omega .$$
Equivalently, $F$ is transversely oriented when there is a nowhere-vanishing
smooth vector field $X$ on $M$ transverse to $F$, that is, $X_p\notin D_p$ for
every $p\in M$.

The two formulations are equivalent because either object is a trivialization
of the same line bundle. A smooth $1$-form vanishing on $D$ is a section of the
annihilator bundle $D^\circ\subseteq T^*M$
([[def-annihilator-bundle-of-a-distribution]]), which has rank one; vanishing of
this section is an intrinsic condition, so a nowhere-vanishing $\omega$ with
$D=\ker\omega$ is exactly a global frame of $D^\circ$, and a line bundle admits
a nowhere-vanishing section exactly when it is trivial. Dually, a vector field
$X$ transverse to $F$ descends to a nowhere-vanishing section of the normal line
bundle $TM/D$, with the normalizations $\omega(X)=1$ identifying the two
trivializations pointwise. Thus transverse orientability is exactly triviality
of the normal line bundle $TM/D$. When $M$ is closed this triviality is a
genuine restriction, related to orientability of $M$ and of the foliation
([[def-orientable-manifold]]).

On a transversely oriented codimension-one foliation the local transversals to
$F$ are ordered: in a foliation chart the sign of $\omega$ orients the
one-dimensional transverse coordinate, and this orientation is respected by all
plaque transports, so the transverse direction is globally coherent along each
leaf. All foliations of this pair are smooth and regular, and it is regularity
together with a co-orientation that the stability theorems below use.

The passage between the two smooth global objects uses only the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ partition-of-unity input ([[thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds]]). Given $\omega$, locally choose smooth transverse fields $X_i$ with $\omega(X_i)=1$ and patch them with a subordinate partition $\rho_i$; then $X=\sum_i\rho_iX_i$ satisfies $\omega(X)=1$. Conversely, given transverse $X$, choose local annihilator forms $\omega_i$ normalized by $\omega_i(X)=1$ and patch them the same way. Their sum annihilates $D$ and evaluates to one on $X$, so its kernel is exactly $D$. This supplies the lift from the normal line to actual smooth fields/forms rather than treating the lift as automatic.
entry.strategy: Specialise the published vocabulary: $D=TF$ is the rank-$(n-1)$ subbundle associated with the regular foliation atlas, and the annihilator bundle construction gives the line subbundle $D^0\subseteq T^*M$; a nowhere-vanishing 1-form with $D=\ker\omega$ is a global frame of $D^0$, which is exactly triviality of the normal line bundle $TM/D$. The vector-field form follows from the 1-form form by pointwise duality ($\omega\leftrightarrow X$ with $\omega(X)=1$), and the ordering of a local transversal by $\operatorname{sign}\omega$ is the orientation of the transversal as an oriented 1-manifold. No choice principle beyond the standing $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the smooth-distribution setting is used.

entry.title: A nonempty compact connected one-dimensional manifold without boundary is a circle
entry.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $X$ be a nonempty
compact connected one-dimensional topological manifold without boundary
([[def-compact-space]], [[def-connected-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Then $X$ is homeomorphic to the circle
$S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$
([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). If in addition $X$ carries a
smooth structure making it a smooth one-manifold without boundary, then $X$ is
diffeomorphic to this circle
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]).

The empty manifold is excluded by the hypothesis: it is compact and connected
under the conventions of this library, but it is not homeomorphic to a circle.
The hypothesis "without boundary" is likewise essential: the closed interval
$[0,1]$ is compact and connected but has boundary points and is not a circle.
entry.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty compact connected one-dimensional topological manifold $X$ without boundary, and the hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[F1] A space is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover; a family of sets is finite when it is empty or consists of $n+1$ sets for some natural number $n$ ([[def-compact-space]]).

[F3] The unit circle is $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$ with the subspace topology and the induced smooth structure ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]).

[F4] Every compact smooth $1$-manifold $W$, possibly with boundary, is diffeomorphic to a finite disjoint union of copies of the circle and of the closed interval $[0,1]$; a circle component contributes no boundary point and an interval component contributes exactly two ([[lem-boundary-of-a-compact-one-manifold-has-even-cardinality]]).

[F5] A topological space is connected when it admits no separation by two disjoint nonempty open sets; a homeomorphism carries connectedness and boundary points to connectedness and boundary points, and a continuous image of a connected space is connected ([[def-connected-space]], [[def-topological-manifold-with-boundary]]).

[F6] Closed bounded real intervals are compact, continuous images of compact spaces are compact and compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed ([[thm-heine-borel-characterisation-r]], [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]], [[thm-compact-subset-of-a-hausdorff-space-is-closed]]). Real intervals are connected ([[thm-connected-subsets-of-r-are-intervals]]). Finite closed pasting gives continuity, and a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism ([[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]], [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct, by a finite interval cut and the locally proved smooth classification.

1.1 Choose coordinate arcs with smaller closed coordinate intervals whose interiors cover $X$. Compactness gives finitely many such intervals $K_i$, each embedded in its coordinate chart. Their images are compact and closed by [F6]. Let $F$ be the finite set of all their endpoints; it is nonempty. In each $K_i$, cutting at its finitely many points of $F$ gives finitely many open intervals. Each such interval $C$ is open in $X$, connected by [F6], and closed in $X\setminus F$, because its compact closure is the corresponding embedded closed interval with its two endpoints in $F$. If two cut intervals meet, connectedness and this open-and-closed property force each to lie in the other, so they are equal. Every point of $X\setminus F$ lies in one of them, since it lies in some $K_i$ and is not an endpoint. Thus the distinct cut intervals form a finite partition of $X\setminus F$, each with an embedded closed-arc closure and two distinct endpoints in $F$. [F1, F5, F6, given, construct]

2.1 At any $v\in F$, choose a sufficiently small coordinate interval containing no other point of $F$. Its two half-intervals lie in two incident cut-arc ends, and every incident arc approaching $v$ occupies one of these two sides. Hence exactly two ends meet at $v$. Start with one arc and follow its other endpoint by the unique other incident arc. Since there are finitely many vertices, a vertex repeats. The first repeated vertex is the starting vertex: a different earlier vertex already had both incident ends used on its first visit, so arrival from a previously unvisited vertex would require a third end. The resulting cyclic chain uses both ends at each of its vertices. Its union is closed, being a finite union of compact closed arcs, and open: interior points have interval neighbourhoods, and at its vertices both local sides belong to that union. It is nonempty, so connectedness of $X$ makes this cyclic chain all of $X$. This proves the cycle conclusion also when two different arcs have the same pair of endpoints. [F5, F6, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Divide $S^1$ into the same finite number of consecutive closed angular arcs and map them, in cyclic order, onto the closed coordinate arcs of step 2.1, parametrizing each by its interval coordinate. Adjacent endpoints agree and only these endpoints are identified. Finite closed pasting gives a continuous bijection $S^1\to X$; [F6] makes it a homeomorphism. This proves the topological assertion without importing the classification of all connected topological one-manifolds. [F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 If $X$ has a smooth structure, use the locally proved smooth classification [F4]. Its finitely many components are circles or closed intervals. Empty boundary excludes every interval; nonemptiness and connectedness leave exactly one circle. Thus the smooth assertion is a diffeomorphism with the standard circle. The finite topological construction used no extra choice; the countable-choice hypothesis is inherited from the smooth supplier. The empty manifold and the closed interval fail the respective explicit hypotheses, as stated. [F3, F4, F5, step 3.1] ∎

entry.title: The Axiom of Choice implies countable choice
entry.statement:
Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For every sequence
$(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a sequence
$(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $a_n\in A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus the
Axiom of Choice implies the pair-local countable choice principle
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]).
entry.strategy: Apply full AC to the family $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$. The resulting choice function is exactly the witness required by [[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]], since AC supplies a choice function for every indexed family of nonempty sets ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Thus full AC implies countable choice.

entry.title: C¹ foliation charts preserve plaque equivalence and transverse orientation
entry.statement:
For a $C^1$ foliation atlas as in
[[def-c1-regular-codimension-one-foliation-and-transverse-orientation]], the
plaque-chain relation is an equivalence relation that is independent of chart
refinement and of the choice of foliation atlas presenting the same slices,
and the transverse orientation condition is independent of the chosen signed
transverse coordinates.
entry.strategy: On each overlap the transition sends a plaque $t_\alpha=c$ to the plaque $t_\beta=h_{\beta\alpha}(c)$ because $t_\beta$ depends only on $t_\alpha$; the inverse overlap has the same form, so finite plaque chains are unchanged by refinement and reversal. Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are respectively the one-plaque chain, reversal of a chain, and concatenation. A change of signed transverse coordinate has positive derivative exactly when it preserves the chosen one-dimensional orientation; positivity is preserved under composition and inversion. These checks make the atlas and coorientation definition independent of representatives.

entry.title: C¹ germs of local diffeomorphisms form a group
entry.statement:
Composition of representatives induces a well-defined group operation on
$\operatorname{Diff}^1_x(T)$; the germ of the identity is a two-sided unit,
every germ has a two-sided inverse, and the germs of positive derivative in an
oriented coordinate form the subgroup
$\operatorname{Diff}^{1,+}_x(T)$.
entry.strategy: If representatives agree near $x$, then after restricting to a common neighbourhood their composites agree, so composition is well defined on germs. Associativity and the identity law hold on representatives. The $C^1$ inverse function theorem ([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]) supplies a $C^1$ local inverse; its germ is independent of the representative because any two representatives agreeing near $x$ have the same inverse on a smaller image neighbourhood. The chain rule gives $(f\circ g)'(x)=f'(x)g'(x)$ and $(f^{-1})'(x)=1/f'(x)$, so positive derivative is closed under composition and inverse.

entry.title: A compact C¹ foliation leaf is an embedded hypersurface
entry.statement:
Let $F$ be a $C^1$ codimension-one foliation of a smooth Hausdorff manifold
$M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let $L$ be a leaf of
$F$ that is compact in its intrinsic leaf-manifold topology
([[def-compact-space]]). Then the inclusion $L\hookrightarrow M$ is a $C^1$
embedding, so $L$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface of $M$.
entry.strategy: In the intrinsic leaf charts supplied by [[def-c1-regular-codimension-one-foliation-and-transverse-orientation]], inclusion is an injective $C^1$ immersion. The inclusion is a continuous bijection from compact $L$ to its image in the Hausdorff space $M$, so it is a homeomorphism onto its image ([[def-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]). At each point, choose ambient and leaf coordinates and project onto $n-1$ ambient coordinates on which the derivative has full rank. The resulting map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ has invertible derivative, so the $C^1$ inverse function theorem expresses the immersed image locally as a $C^1$ graph ([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]). The homeomorphism onto the image ensures an ambient neighborhood meets only this local branch. Thus the inclusion is an embedding in the slice-chart sense of [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]].

entry.title: Countable choice is equivalent to nonempty countable products
entry.statement:
For every sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets, there exists a
choice function $c$ with domain $\mathbb N$ and $c(n)\in A_n$ for every
$n\in\mathbb N$ if and only if the product $\prod_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n$ is
nonempty. Thus the sequence formulation of
[[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]] and the nonempty-product
formulation of the same principle are equivalent.
entry.strategy: By [[def-product-of-an-indexed-family]], an element of $\prod_n A_n$ is a function on $\mathbb N$ whose value at each $n$ belongs to $A_n$; this is exactly the choice function in [[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]] ([[def-function]], [[def-choice-function]]). The two formulations therefore imply each other by identifying the function with the same ordered assignment of coordinates.

entry.title: Gluing manifolds with boundary along a boundary diffeomorphism
entry.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $W_1,W_2$ be smooth
$n$-manifolds with nonempty boundary ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]]) and let
$\varphi:\partial W_1\to\partial W_2$ be a diffeomorphism
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]). Then the
quotient
$$W:=W_1\sqcup W_2\big/\{\,x\sim\varphi(x):x\in\partial W_1\,\}$$
carries a smooth structure for which the two inclusions $W_i\hookrightarrow W$
are smooth embeddings onto their images, making $W$ a smooth $n$-manifold
without boundary. Fixing collars fixes this smooth structure; the smooth
gluing type is independent of the collar choices, up to diffeomorphism. If
moreover each $W_i$ carries a regular codimension-$q$ foliation $F_i$ tangent to
$\partial W_i$ ([[def-regular-foliation-atlas]]) and $\varphi$ carries the
foliation of $\partial W_1$ induced by $F_1$ to that induced by $F_2$
([[thm-the-boundary-is-a-closed-embedded-smooth-n-minus-one-manifold]]), and their tangent plane fields have matching smooth jets in signed collar
coordinates, then the $F_i$ glue to a regular codimension-$q$ foliation $F$ of $W$ restricting to
$F_i$ on $W_i$. Here matching jets means the following explicit local condition. Identify the collars with $\partial W_1\times(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ using $\varphi$ and opposite normal signs. Let $E$ be the common rank-$(n-q)$ tangent distribution on the seam, and choose a complement to $E$ there, extended constantly in the signed collar. Each side's nearby plane field is the graph of a smooth linear map $A_-(z,s)$ or $A_+(z,s)$ from $E_z$ to this complement. Require $\partial_s^j A_-(z,0)=\partial_s^j A_+(z,0)$ for every $j\ge0$. Equality of boundary foliations alone does not imply this condition and does not suffice for smooth foliated gluing.
entry.strategy:
Choose collar neighbourhoods $C_i\cong\partial W_i\times[0,1)$ with $\partial W_i$ corresponding to $\partial W_i\times\{0\}$ ([[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]). Near the glued locus model charts on the collar of $W_1$ as $U\times(-1,0]$ and on the collar of $W_2$ as $\varphi(U)\times[0,1)$, glued by $(x,s)\sim(\varphi(x),-s)$; the resulting charts are smooth and agree with the given atlases on overlaps of collars, giving a smooth atlas and Hausdorff second countable quotient when the $W_i$ are second countable (compactness of the $W_i$ in the applications makes the quotient compact). For the foliation claim, the collar charts can be chosen adapted to $F_i$ because $F_i$ is tangent to $\partial W_i$; the gluing identification then carries plaques to plaques, so the local models glue to a regular foliation atlas of $W$. Only the standing $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used.

Here $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ denotes the countable-choice principle [[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]].

entry.title: A closed smooth manifold has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex
entry.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a closed smooth
manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Then $M$ has the homotopy type of a finite
CW complex ([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]).
entry.strategy: Let $c_1<\dots<c_k$ be the critical values of $f$; they are distinct because $f$ is excellent ([[def-morse-function-and-excellent-morse-function]]) and finitely many because $M$ is compact ([[cor-a-morse-function-on-a-compact-manifold-has-finitely-many-critical-points]]). Choose regular values $a_0<c_1<a_1<c_2<\dots<c_k<a_k$ with $a_0<\min f$ and $a_k>\max f$; this is possible because only finitely many values are critical, and then $M^{a_0}=\varnothing$ and $M^{a_k}=M$. For each $j$ the compact band $f^{-1}([a_{j-1},a_j])$ has regular boundary values and contains exactly one critical point $p_j$, nondegenerate by the Morse condition, so the one-critical-point compact-band form of the handle-attachment theorem ([[cor-one-critical-point-cell-attachment-homotopy-type]]) gives a homotopy equivalence $M^{a_j}\simeq M^{a_{j-1}}\cup e^{\lambda_j}$ with one cell attached along the transported attaching sphere, compatible with the lower sublevel up to homotopy of pairs. Inducting on $j$ and using [[def-cell-attachment-by-a-characteristic-map]] and the closure-finiteness and weak topology of [[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]], each sublevel $M^{a_j}$ has the homotopy type of the finite CW complex $X_j=X_{j-1}\cup e^{\lambda_j}$; since $M=M^{a_k}$, the manifold $M$ has the homotopy type of the finite CW complex $X_k$ with one $\lambda_j$-cell for each $j$. Finiteness of the cell set is finiteness of the critical set. The axiom of choice is consumed through [[cor-every-compact-smooth-manifold-admits-an-excellent-morse-function]], and the attachments use the countable-choice hypothesis of the published handle-attachment items, which follows from full AC by [[lem-axiom-of-choice-implies-countable-choice]].

entry.title: A non-closed leaf of a codimension-one foliation meets a closed transversal
entry.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $F$ be a smooth cooriented codimension-one foliation of a smooth manifold $M$, and let $A$ be a leaf that is not a closed subset of $M$. There is a smooth embedded circle transverse to $F$ that meets $A$.

The circle need not lie in every prescribed open neighborhood of $A$; the localization claim is false. The stronger finite-compact-barrier version needed in compact ambient manifolds is constructed directly in the global closedness lemma.
entry.strategy:
Follow the proof of Calegari, Lemma 4.24 (printed p. 155): a non-closed leaf accumulates somewhere, so there is a product chart $U$ meeting $\lambda$ in at least two plaques through which one passes from one plaque of $\lambda$ to another along a short transversal segment $\tau$; let $\gamma_0$ be an embedded arc in $\lambda$ joining the two endpoints of $\tau$ and contained in a neighbourhood on which the product structure is defined. Replacing one of the two segments of $\tau$ (the one on the negative side of $\gamma_0$) by the graph $\tau'(t)=(\gamma_0(t),t)$ inside a rectangle foliated by transversals gives an embedded closed curve $\tau'\cup(\tau\smallsetminus\tau^-)$ that is transverse to $F$ and meets $\lambda$; the isotopy from $\tau^-$ to $\tau'$ can be performed in an arbitrarily small neighbourhood of $\gamma_0$ and of $U$, so $\gamma$ lies in an arbitrarily small neighbourhood of $\lambda$. Only the standing $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used.

Here $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ denotes the countable-choice principle [[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]].

entry.title: Holonomy of a C¹ foliation is a representation into C¹ transverse germs
entry.statement:
Let $F$ be a transversely oriented $C^1$ codimension-one foliation, $L$ a
leaf, $x\in L$, and $T$ a local $C^1$ transversal to $F$ at $x$. Plaque
transport along leafwise loops defines a homomorphism
$$\rho_x:\pi_1(L,x)\to\operatorname{Diff}^{1,+}_x(T)$$
that is independent of the chosen chains of foliation charts and invariant
under leafwise homotopies relative to endpoints.
entry.strategy: A finite chain of C¹ foliation charts transports a sufficiently small transversal by a finite composition of C¹ transverse coordinate changes, hence gives a C¹ local diffeomorphism germ; coorientation makes every factor orientation-preserving ([[def-c1-regular-codimension-one-foliation-and-transverse-orientation]], [[def-c1-germ-of-a-local-diffeomorphism-at-a-point]], [[lem-c1-germs-of-local-diffeomorphisms-form-a-group]]). Refining a chart chain leaves the composite germ unchanged. For a leafwise homotopy of paths, compactness of the parameter square gives a finite subdivision into rectangles each lying in one foliation chart; transport around each rectangle is the identity because the transverse coordinate is constant along plaques. Cancelling internal edges proves homotopy invariance. Concatenating loops concatenates the transverse maps, so $\rho_x$ is a homomorphism, with composition order fixed by the path-concatenation convention of [[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]].
